overview: This file traces the recovery, capacity, and allocation of Japan’s pulp, paper, and especially newsprint industries under the Allied occupation from 1947 through 1949. It combines production reports and statistical tables prepared by SCAP’s Natural Resources and Economic and Scientific Sections with State Department despatches on mill capacity, shortages of pulpwood, coal, chemicals, and electricity, and the loss of prewar raw-material sources. A second major strand concerns the politically contentious rationing of scarce newsprint, including American Federation of Labor allegations that Communist publications received preferential treatment, SCAP’s detailed rebuttal, and a later political-party allocation plan. The opening telegram about a Siamese textile-purchasing mission appears to have been included through a cross-reference rather than because it concerns paper manufacturing directly.

subfiles.title: Telegram approving a Siamese textile mission to Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for the U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.about: The Department approves the entry into Japan of two Siamese representatives seeking to arrange the purchase and shipment of Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: The telegram repeats Bangkok’s March 18 report that the Siamese government planned to send Luang Prakit Sahakorn and Nai Krdt Tunkaswat to negotiate with SCAP. Their mission concerned shipping Japanese textiles to Bangkok and handling related arrangements. The Department approved their entry subject to SCAP’s concurrence and directed that Bangkok be informed.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1023 on February–March pulp and paper production
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports improving Japanese pulp and paper output and supplies March 1947 production statistics requested by the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: A Natural Resources Section memorandum reports that March paper production reached a new occupation-era high, 16 percent above February, while pulp production rose 35.5 percent. Particularly large increases occurred in rayon B pulp, unbleached kraft, groundwood, and unbleached sulphite, and the report credits cooperation with Japanese industry rather than coercion. The accompanying table records March totals of 23,518 short tons of pulp and 24,168 short tons of paper.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for Despatch No. 1108
subfiles.to: Department of State action office and DC/R
subfiles.about: This administrative sheet designates the attached copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 1108 as the record copy replacing an unreturned original.
subfiles.summary: The form states that the original action copy was not returned to Central Records and directs that the substitute record copy be returned to DC/R for filing. It identifies the underlying item as Tokyo Despatch No. 1108, filed under 894.656/6-1147, and bears a February 16, 1948 filming stamp.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1108 transmitting “Newsprint in Japan”
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a SCAP preliminary study of Japan’s newsprint industry.
subfiles.summary: Five copies of Natural Resources Section Preliminary Study No. 11, dated June 6, 1947, are transmitted. The study reportedly covers the history of Japanese newsprint, mills and manufacturing methods, forest resources, capacity, output, and import-export statistics. The referenced study and its six statistical tables are not reproduced in this file.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1223/1283 transmitting March–May production reports
subfiles.from: Counselor of Mission, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards two Natural Resources Section memoranda on Japanese pulp and paper production in March, April, and May 1947.
subfiles.summary: The Counselor of Mission refers to Despatch No. 1023 and encloses memoranda dated May 17 and June 21 for the Office of International Trade. The cover page numbers the despatch No. 1223, while the enclosure headings identify it as No. 1283. The enclosures extend the monthly production series through May 1947.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on March–April 1947 pulp and paper production
subfiles.from: Harold R. Murdock, Natural Resources Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains apparent April production declines caused by altered reporting periods and compares March and April pulp and paper output.
subfiles.summary: The Economic Stabilization Board required mills to report production as of the twentieth of each month, making April figures from the dominant Oji Paper Manufacturing Company appear artificially low. Murdock nevertheless identifies a probable real shift from newsprint toward other printing papers, while rayon pulp and unbleached kraft increased. The attached table compares detailed pulp and paper categories and explains the grades and uses of rayon and kraft pulp.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on April–May 1947 pulp and paper production
subfiles.from: Harold R. Murdock, Natural Resources Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.about: The memorandum compares April and May output and examines a sharp May decline in rayon pulp production.
subfiles.summary: Rayon pulp output fell severely in May, which Japanese producers attributed to shortages of coal, bleaching powder, and electric power. Murdock notes that increased unbleached sulphite production does not fully support that explanation and suggests that the industry may have favored printing paper at the expense of rayon pulp. The table shows overall May increases in total pulp and paper production despite the collapse in rayon B output.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 119 surveying 1947 newsprint production, exports, and imports
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch responds to a circular inquiry with estimates of Japan’s effective, installed, and near-term newsprint capacity.
subfiles.summary: The mission forwards a completed chart on the world distribution of newsprint in 1947, although the chart itself is not present here. SCAP’s Economic and Scientific Section estimated effective Japanese capacity at 175,000 short tons and potentially rehabilitated installed capacity at 217,728 short tons, requiring at least a year of repairs. Given contemporary fuel and pulpwood allocations, first-quarter 1948 production was expected to reach only about 75 percent of effective capacity.

subfiles.title: State Department inquiry about alleged pro-Communist newsprint allocations
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, signed George C. Marshall
subfiles.to: SCAP, Tokyo, for the Acting U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.about: The Department requests information and comment on Matthew Woll’s accusation that scarce Japanese newsprint was being distributed disproportionately to Communist publications and unions.
subfiles.summary: The telegram condenses a June 22 letter from AFL official Matthew Woll listing allocations to the Communist daily Red Flag and several other Communist-associated publications. Woll argues that these allocations were disproportionate to Communist electoral strength and membership and that Communist-controlled unions also received an excessive share. He claims democratic unions consequently had to purchase paper on the black market, and the Department asks SCAP for material on which to base a reply.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on newsprint allocations to Communist and labor publications
subfiles.to: Department of the Army and U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: SCAP explains and defends Japan’s newsprint allocation system while outlining contemplated reallocations and additional supplies for labor-union publications.
subfiles.summary: SCAP states that scarce paper was prioritized for textbooks and general daily newspapers, which were themselves restricted to two pages. Akahata received only one-half of one percent of newspaper allocations, although SCAP acknowledges that this was generous relative to Communist Party strength and resulted partly from allocations being frozen at the end of 1946. Officials were considering redistributing all party-organ paper according to the latest election but feared that singling out Akahata would create sympathy for the Communist Party. The telegram also reports allocations to 54 labor magazines and a plan to provide unions with 200,000 pounds of newsprint monthly for four-page weeklies.

subfiles.title: SCAP telegram on 1948 newsprint statistics and the 1949 forecast
subfiles.to: Department of the Army, for passage to the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: The telegram supplies Japanese newsprint capacity, production, trade, and forecast figures requested for calendar year 1948.
subfiles.summary: SCAP reports capacity of 173,300 short tons, actual 1948 production of 111,799 tons, no exports, and imports of 3,365 tons from the Soviet-controlled Sakhalin Islands. It identifies pulpwood as the principal production constraint. Before the war Japan had obtained most of its imported pulpwood from Formosa, Korea, and Sakhalin, sources now lost to it; estimated 1949 newsprint output was 115,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 259 on political-party newsprint allocations
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports a proposed newsprint-allocation plan for Japanese political-party publications, apparently intended to begin on May 1, 1949.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR is badly damaged, but it indicates that newsprint was to be allocated under a new plan affecting party publications. It specifically names the Democratic Party and Social Democratic Party and refers to the Newsprint Allocations Board. The despatch appears to promise or request further details concerning the plan and its application.

interest: The file is especially valuable for its nearly month-by-month view of early postwar industrial recovery and for showing how SCAP interpreted production figures distorted by changing reporting periods. It also documents the political consequences of material scarcity: newsprint rationing became entangled with American labor politics, Japanese party competition, anti-Communism, and concern that suppressing Communist media might prove counterproductive. The statistics on lost prewar pulpwood sources connect Japan’s paper shortage directly to the territorial and economic transformation produced by defeat. Administrative features—including the substitute record-copy sheet, inconsistent despatch numbering, missing studies and charts, and the unrelated Siamese textile cross-reference—also illuminate how the State Department’s decimal files were assembled and maintained.
